entries.misconception: There are no facts in fiction.
entries.identify: Relate a story or fable that is based on something factual. Ask the learners to identify the facts in the story.
entries.overcome: Ask learners to make up their own story or fable, based on facts they know about salt. This is also a good extension activity.

entries.misconception: Fables must have animal characters.
entries.identify: Learners should remember the essential features of fables from prior learning. They often remember animal characters. Talk about fables they know. Read one or two with animal characters to remind them.
entries.overcome: Read a wider range of fables to the learners, including ones without animals. Reading fables from around the world – often classified as folk tales, traditional tales or even fairy tales – will help focus on the lesson learnt rather than the animal characters.

entries.misconception: Modal verbs have tenses.
entries.identify: Invite learners to try to form the past and future tenses using modal verbs.
entries.overcome: Modal verbs do not change in form to make different tenses. The past tense is created by using a modal verb + have + –ed form (or past participle) of the verb that follows. Demonstrate with a few verbs and then discuss how expressing possibility encompasses the future.

entries.misconception: Possessive adjectives and pronouns are the same thing.
entries.identify: Ask learners whether the noun appears with the word they think is a possessive pronoun. If it does, ask if it is giving more information about a noun. If so, it must be an adjective.
entries.overcome: Practice and familiarity will help learners overcome confusion. Activity 2 provides practice. Activate learners' awareness by regularly doing spot quizzes on possessive pronouns/adjectives.

entries.misconception: Idioms and proverbs are the same thing.
entries.identify: Ask learners what different proverbs and idioms mean. The proverbs should be easily understood whereas the idioms may need to be learnt.
entries.overcome: Link proverbs clearly to a message or lesson. Show how idiomatic language adds colour and interest to writing but does not teach a lesson. Use the listening activity as practice with proverbs.

entries.identify: Keep the focus on the words actually spoken. Keep asking if the character actually said those words or whether someone is reporting what they said.
entries.overcome: Use the direct speech activities beginning with the speech bubbles in Activity 1 to show exactly what words are said. Use the Workbook for additional practice.

entries.misconception: A discussion forum is the same as a debate.
entries.identify: Ask learners what they think a discussion forum and a debate are. Find out if they have seen any TV debates, for example, with politicians. They may also have watched discussion forums discussing, for example a sports event, with the panel giving their ideas and opinions.
entries.overcome: Emphasise that a discussion forum, while incorporating discussion on a topic, does not have teams of people for and against a particular statement. Choose a recent event in your region. Ask learners’ opinions on what they think about it and show how a discussion forum is built up.

entries.misconception: Editing and proofreading means correcting mistakes.
entries.identify: While identifying and correcting mistakes is important (e.g. for spellings), editing and improving drafts is much more than that. Ask learners what sort of things they do when editing (link to any success criteria). Make a list on the board and add suggestions of your own if necessary.
entries.overcome: Encourage learners to focus on success criteria or criteria for the writing task. They can also use the editing checklists in the Learner’s Book or Worksheets 5.4 and 5.5 which give different insights into editing.

entries.misconception: Astronaut only describes someone who goes into space.
entries.identify: Ask learners to look up the word astronaut. Explain that an astronaut is someone trained to travel or work in a spacecraft, but who may never actually do so.
entries.overcome: Show examples or invite learners to research astronauts who work in space and on the ground. This will help them see that an astronaut can be both.

entries.misconception: All adverbs end in –ly
entries.identify: Write a list of regular and irregular adverbs on the board (e.g. happily, quickly, often and never). Ask learners to use each one in a sentence and ask what the word is doing in each case.
entries.overcome: When they see that all the words on the board add information to verbs, ask the purpose of each one (how, when, why and where) and familiarise them with how to tell a word is an adverb even if it does not end in –ly.

entries.misconception: All online information is correct, reliable, true and up to date.
entries.identify: Discuss online safety. Remind learners that not everything they read and see is correct, true or reliable – even in newspapers. Talk about reliable sites and why it is important to stick to well-reviewed sites and tell an adult when they go online.
entries.overcome: Learners write a list of ‘dos and don’ts’ for reading material online. Display a list of well-reviewed, reliable, age-appropriate sites that learners can use if they go online to look for information.

entries.misconception: You have to be in the same room to interview someone.
entries.identify: Talk about different ways to communicate with and interview someone, especially if you cannot be in the same room. These days we can use the telephone or a computer/tablet which means we can speak to someone far away – even in space.
entries.overcome: Show examples of interviews with astronauts in space and discuss how they take place. Discuss how this type of interview differs from one with someone in the same room.

entries.misconception: A biography is only for famous people and is always a book.
entries.identify: Talk about the purpose of a biography. Ask: Who has a biography? Why? Can anyone have a biography? (yes) Are all biographies published as books? (no) Are they always long? (no – some are very short).
entries.overcome: Have a display of biographies of different people that the learners may or may not recognise. Include books, newspaper articles, obituaries, mini bios and author biographies on the back of books.

entries.misconception: Adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses are the same.
entries.identify: Display this example and ask learners to notice the difference: As a child, she dreamt of going into space. = phrase (no verb) As she grew up, she dreamt of going into space. = clause (verb)
entries.overcome: Practise identifying adverbial phrases and clauses. Focus on finding the finite verb, e.g. wishing to be an astronaut is not a clause because wishing on its own is not a finite verb.

entries.misconception: One rough draft is enough.
entries.identify: Remind learners that most authors have to edit and rewrite their novels many times before they are accepted.
entries.overcome: Demonstrate on the board how to ‘fix’ or improve the text one sentence at a time. Learners can use the editing checklists (Worksheets 5.4 and 5.5) to edit their work and that of their peers. Encourage them to follow this process more than once until they feel their written work is their best effort.

entries.misconception: Language has always been the same.
entries.identify: Use The Jungle Book extract to identify the unfamiliar pronouns. Ask learners if the pronouns are wrong. Encourage them to recall other historical literature from other stages and talk about why it is different if written long ago or was written in the style of long ago.
entries.overcome: Use the extracts to show that not only has the style of speaking changed from historical times but words also have changed and fallen out of common usage. Discuss how new words are created all the time – especially ones relating to the digital revolution. Such words may be familiar and ordinary now, but a generation ago, these words may not have existed or may have been used in a different context (e.g. smartphone).

entries.misconception: Standard English is difficult to write.
entries.identify: There is no mystery about standard English. It is merely correct spelling, grammar and punctuation. Standard English follows the rules whereas spoken English is more flexible. If learners feel that standard English is something that they are unsure about, remind them that it will be in their reading books and all their textbooks, which makes them in fact easier to understand.
entries.overcome: Demystify standard English by focusing on its features and consistently differentiating for learners the difference between standard English narrative and dialogue. Where dialogue breaks the rules of standard English, point it out to learners and ask how it would be written in standard English instead. The more they engage with standard English and its core rules, the more familiar it will become. It will sound right and be right.

entries.misconception: Screenplays and playscripts are the same.
entries.identify: Ask learners to list the differences between a play and film (both have actors and sets, etc., but films take place in a real-life location). The important difference is the audience. Plays have a fixed audience, whereas people can watch films on a variety of different media. The camera work can materially affect how the audience perceives the action (close-ups, wide-angle and so on).
entries.overcome: Ask learners what directors of films have to consider over and above what a play director has to consider. The difference is mostly to do with a live production as opposed to a film where the performance is not live but is filmed bit by bit with a variety of camera angles, lighting and work. Encourage learners to think of films they have seen and then to think about how they were filmed and staged.

entries.overcome: Use Activity 3 to help differentiate. Focus especially on legends having some link to historical events even if the story has moved far away from the reality and become embellished with fantastical creatures such as dragons or gigantic beasts.

entries.misconception: First- and third- person narrative are difficult to tell apart.
entries.identify: Use independent learners as well as texts in the Learner’s Book to ask learners who is telling the story. Is it one of the characters? Or is it someone who seems to be on the outside of the story looking in?
entries.overcome: Help learners to notice the common features when a character narrates the story. Frequent use of I, we, my, our, mine and ours in narrative as well as in dialogue indicates that a character is telling the story – so first person. An outside narrator has to relate what is happening and so uses more third-person personal and possessive pronouns and adjectives.

entries.overcome: Focus on the spelling rules for plurals, using Activity 1 to guide you. Show that while s is added, unless the word has a fully irregular plural form, it may be preceded by e or even change f to ves.

entries.misconception: You can use any connective to form a complex sentence.

entries.identify: Read the poem several times with learners and get them to list rhyming words in the poem.
entries.overcome: Source other poems with internal rhymes or assonance to embed the notion that rhymes can also be internal. Use the Workbook for further practice.

entries.misconception: Words that are spelled the same always rhyme.
entries.identify: Ask learners what letter combinations can be used to create certain sounds – especially the long vowel sounds.
entries.overcome: Focus on one of two vowel sounds – particularly the sounds appearing in the poem, e.g. oo. Write a list of words on the board e.g. wood, poor, moo, stood, brood, school and spoon. Invite learners to classify them according to sound, e.g. spoon and school. Then invite them to think of other words that rhyme with each, e.g. wood, should; moo, shoe; spoon, strewn to show that rhyming is about sound, not spelling.

entries.misconception: Poems need punctuation like sentences.
entries.identify: Check the context – the preposition must be followed by a noun. Look at a wide range of poems in the classroom and focus on the punctuation and capital letters.
entries.overcome: Use the poem ‘Once the Wind’ to show that poems can have no punctuation at all. Encourage learners to explain the effect of no punctuation – this is a matter of personal opinion. There is no right answer. Ask learners why they think the poet did not use any.

entries.misconception: Clauses and phrases are the same.
entries.identify: Talk about how to extend simple sentences and ask: What is being added? Is it groups of words to add detail without a verb? Or is it a group of words that contain a verb?
entries.overcome: When you work with multi-clause sentences, point out whether they are two main clauses joined by a connective or whether one of the clauses is dependent (often an adverbial clause). Use Activity 1 and the Language focus box to help learners identify phrases from clauses.

entries.overcome: If learners begin writing the synopsis using the past tense, let them finish before reviewing their work and discussing the tense with them, encouraging them to change the verbs into the present tense.

entries.misconception: Homonyms and homophones are the same thing.
entries.identify: Ask learners what a homophone is and to give examples. Now write a homonym on the board such as wave and ask learners what the word means. When they come up with several definitions, explain it is known as a homonym.
entries.overcome: Help learners understand the difference between a homophone and a homonym. Use a breakdown of the word homophone to help them remember – phone comes from the ancient Greek relating to sound and a homophone sounds the same rather than being spelled the same.

entries.misconception: Facts and opinions are interchangeable.
entries.identify: Ask learners to explain what a fact is and what an opinion is, giving examples. Then ask: How are they different?
entries.overcome: Keep asking learners whether something is a fact: Is it true? Can it be proved? Then ask their opinion on a range of things such as Should learners wear school uniform? Each time they answer, get them to give a reason why they think that and then give reasons why the opposite opinion could also be held. This will help them realise that there can be more than one opinion on something.

entries.misconception: Good writing is hard.
entries.identify: Ask learners what they think good writing is like: What are its features? Then ask what they find easy or difficult about writing stories. Collate what they find difficult on the board.
entries.overcome: Discuss each item that learners find hard and try to turn it into a process: they do not have to write a perfect first draft as the real work comes in editing and improving it. Encourage them to focus on just one or two aspects at a time rather than trying to get everything perfect.

entries.misconception: People recounting the same events include the same details.
entries.identify: Invite two or three learners to recount an event that they all participated in, e.g. something that happened at assembly or in the classroom. Listen to each account and then invite the rest of the class to identify differences in their accounts.
entries.overcome: Help learners to realise that people remembering events differently or different details does not mean they are not telling the truth, although someone could be telling just some of the truth. Use the voices to show learners that when recounting the same events, different characters focus on different aspects – they have different perspectives.

entries.overcome: Use the discussion to help learners see that authors can manage flashbacks in a variety of ways, including separate chapters and differentiated text, e.g. italics. entries.overcome: Use the poem The River to show that stanzas do not have to match each other in length. Encourage learners to become aware of how poems are structured throughout the unit and discuss possible reasons for choosing different-length stanzas.

entries.misconception: Listening for information is difficult.
entries.identify: Ask learners whether it is easier to listen for information or to listen for imagery, as when listening to a poem. Find out what makes listening for information challenging, e.g. the speed of the audio or too much detail.
entries.overcome: Use the listening activity to show that listening for information is easier if they follow simple steps. First, learners must read the questions and visualise the sort of answer they are looking for, for example, an age or a reason. Second, they must listen carefully and jot down notes if they are not to hear the audio a second time. Third, they must try to answer the questions with the information they can remember or their notes and identify any missing information to listen out for if the audio is played a second time.

Emphasise that the texts were written some time ago and so what may have seemed impossible then may seem very possible now.

entries.misconception: Compound-complex sentences are difficult to read (or complicated to read) – and simple sentences are easy to read.
entries.identify: Write the following two sentences on the board (or create your own): a A long time ago, in a poor, distant land, a boy worked hard for his family, to feed them well by growing food on their farm. b He went running but he cut the run short because it started raining. Ask learners which of the two sentences they find more complicated to read or understand. Then ask them to identify which is a compound- complex sentence and which is a simple.
entries.overcome: Explain that sentence b is a compound-complex sentence (for example, he went running [clause] but he cut the run short [clause] because it started raining [subordinate clause]). Explain that sentence a is a simple sentence as it contains only one main clause (for example, a boy worked hard).

entries.identify: Ask learners to think about how to distinguish the grammatical subject from the topic or logical subject in example sentences. entries.overcome: Ask learners to change the word order of example sentences that you or they write out. Changing the word order of That book was written by my favourite author to My favourite author wrote that book makes My favourite author the grammatical subject.

entries.identify: Ask learners to write the word ‘sparkle’ on a piece of paper and to insert a hyphen to divide the syllable sounds (for example, spar-kle). entries.misconception: Specific questions are best for getting people to give information.
entries.identify: Ask learners what questions they would ask if they wanted to know more about you, their teacher – for example, Where did you grow up? How old are you?

entries.misconception: A statement is always factual and will not need to be examined for personal opinion or bias.
entries.identify: Write on the board a simple example of a statement that could be mistaken for a fact but is really an opinion: It’s cold in this classroom. Ask learners whether this is a fact or an opinion. Then ask them how they could establish any facts from this statement. Guide them towards a more ‘scientific’ approach – for example, saying that measuring the temperature using a thermometer gives you a fact (the number of degrees), but different people might have different opinions about whether that temperature feels comfortable, or too warm or too cool.
entries.overcome: Ask learners for some other simple examples of statements that might seem to be fact, but on closer examination prove to be opinion. Write the best of these on the board. Point out that the structure of a statement is likely to be the same whether it is fact or opinion. End by asking learners to suggest ways of guarding against mistaking opinions for facts in the future.

entries.misconception: Words can always be broken down into component parts, such as prefixes and suffixes.
entries.identify: Write the words ‘prefix’ and ‘precious’ on the board. Ask learners what these words have in common.
entries.overcome: Ask learners what the word ‘prefix’ means. Invite them to explain how they know. entries.misconception: Knowing the origin (etymology) of a word will always allow you to explain its present-day meaning.
entries.identify: Ask learners for a definition of the word pretty. Check that other learners agree and write this definition on the board (most likely it will be attractive, good-looking, etc.).
entries.overcome: Then, ask learners: What is the meaning of the following sentence? She is a pretty girl. Get several responses from learners. Then, tell them that the etymology of the word pretty is cunning and clever. Explain that it can be useful to know a word’s etymology, but that there is a mistake known as ‘the etymological fallacy’. This is when people assume that the historical meaning of a word will explain its present-day meaning. Finish by emphasising that words often change their meanings over time.

entries.misconception: Poems are always composed in the language of the time when they were written.
entries.identify: Invite learners to look at just the first set of six stanzas of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner in the Learner’s Book. They will see ‘old-fashioned’ (archaic) language such as ‘hath paced’ and ‘thus spake on’. From this they may conclude that, in 1798, when the poem was first published, this was how people wrote and spoke English.
entries.overcome: Explain that the poet – Samuel Taylor Coleridge – was deliberately using language that would certainly have been seen as archaic at the time he wrote the poem. He wanted to give the impression of something ancient and mysterious. Explain that this is another example of how writers choose words and language to create particular effects.

entries.misconception: An argument only refers to people having a disagreement.
entries.identify: Write these two sentences on the board: My brother and sister had an argument and are not speaking to each other now. I listened to each side of the debate and then voted for the argument that persuaded me the most.
entries.overcome: Explain that the second meaning of argument is to give reasons for someone to believe something that they do not already believe. If someone does not already agree with an idea, they may need to be persuaded with reasons to change their view. Those reasons are the arguments.

entries.misconception: Using the term ‘reported speech’ when referring to ‘indirect speech’.
entries.identify: Write a sentence of direct speech on the board, for example: ‘My name is Penny,’ said the girl. Write a sentence of indirect speech, for example: The girl said her name was Penny. Ask learners to identify the type of speech for each sentence. Some learners may refer to the indirect speech as ‘reported speech’. This is incorrect.
entries.overcome: Explain that both sentences are examples of reported speech (direct and indirect speech). The words spoken are being ‘reported’. In the first sentence, the speaker is reporting them ‘directly’. In the second sentence, the speaker’s words are being reported ‘indirectly’ by someone else. Encourage learners to use the terms ’direct’ and ’indirect’ speech’. This will also help avoid confusion when describing the clauses used in direct speech (reported clause and reporting clause).
